newsitem.title: INDIA: India leftists to seek changes in income tax plan.
newsitem.headline: India leftists to seek changes in income tax plan.

text.p: India's communist-led Left Front plans to seek a revision of income tax rate reductions proposed in the budget for 1997/98 (April-March), a senior official of the alliance said on Monday.

"We want to amend the budget proposals on the two higher income groups," said Sitaram Yechury, politburo member of the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M). "The reduction in tax on the lower income groups is, however, acceptable to us."
Former finance minister P. Chidambaram had proposed reducing the tax rate on annual income from 40,000 to 60,000 rupees to 10 percent from 15 percent.
The tax rate on income from 60,000 to 150,000 rupees would be cut to 20 percent from 30 percent, while the rate on incomes above 150,000 rupees would be reduced to 30 percent from 40.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's cabinet decided last week to adopt Chidambaram's budget proposals but left it open to possible amendment in parliament, set to take up the plan during a session starting on Wednesday.

The Congress party, which gives Gujral make-or-break support in parliament, has also criticised the income tax proposals, saying the reductions were too steep. But there was no immediate word from Congress if it planned to seek changes.
The rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party said it had no problems with the income tax proposals but planned to oppose some other measures, party officials said without elaborating.
Yechury said the Left Front, which began discussions on the issue on Monday, would not oppose passage of the Finance Bill, which incorporates the tax and tariff measures for 1997/98.
"We will seek amendments in the Finance Bill before it is put to vote," he said.
The Left Front is comprised of the two main communist parties, the Revolutionary Socialist Party and the Forward Bloc, all components of Gujral's United Front coalition.
